KESTREL Datasets

Four corpora, one provenance chain · what a claim on this site is made of and where each part came from

Four bodies of data sit behind this site, and they are not interchangeable. One is a published threat framework. One is a reference map of the Linux system surface. One is a catalogue of what ordinary binaries can be turned into. One is what the kernel will actually let you watch. A detection claim is only as good as the join between them, so each is kept separate, carries its own provenance, and is described on its own page.

Underneath all four is a discipline rather than a schema: inputs are read-only and never edited in place, a reference corpus is derived from them and never hand-written, and the telemetry a fitted model is tested against is kept out of both. Data crossing from evaluation back into training is the one failure that cannot be seen from the inside.

ATT&CK® Framework
MITRE ATT&CK v19, reduced to its Linux surface and resolved down to analytics and data components. This is the vocabulary every other dataset is joined to, and the source of the event key.
Linux Reference
A cross-referenced map of the system surface — syscalls, error codes, /proc, library symbols, programs, platforms — built in three layers that are documented, observed and inferred, and never merged.
Living off the Land
What a legitimate binary can be made to do: GTFOBins abuse functions, offensive tooling admitted on documented purpose, and a benign baseline so that presence alone is never mistaken for evidence.
eBPF Programs
The capability matrix: which program types exist, what each one may call, where each attaches, and which data components a kernel probe can honestly claim to observe.
